1062-first-project-gutenberg-collection-:
Edgar Allan Poe's best-known tales and poems gather in this early Project Gutenberg volume: murders, burials, ravens, and houses that rot from within. The tales show his range, from the logic of the detective story to the dread of premature burial, while the poems sound his musical gloom.

Poe built his effects with care, and each piece aims at a single mood held to the last line. "The Raven," "The Fall of the House of Usher," and "The Tell-Tale Heart" all appear. The volume gives a strong first shelf of Poe, and it suits readers meeting his dark genius for the first time.
11441-the-solitary-of-juan-fernandez-or-:
Translated from the French by Anne T. Wilbur in 1851, The Solitary of Juan Fernandez tells the real Robinson Crusoe story: Alexander Selkirk, marooned on Juan Fernandez island. Chapters follow Selkirk from college and first love through maritime combats, revolt, degradation, and a free shore, then his inspection of the country. dialogue with a toucan, labors as colonist, study, fishing, administration, and encounters with Marimonda, ending in deliverance and return.

The author of Picciola frames Selkirk's solitude as both adventure and moral reflection, asking what is wanting to happiness. The book corrects Defoe's fiction with a documented life. Readers who know Crusoe will enjoy meeting its original, stranger and more solitary than the novel.
13978-the-horse-shoe:
Edward G. Flight retold the true legend of St. Dunstan and the Devil in this small book, showing how the horse-shoe became a charm against witchcraft. George Cruikshank illustrated it, with engravings by John Thompson. A third edition appeared in 1871, after earlier success. Flight's preface notes expressive silence and popular demand.

Dunstan, in his cell, makes mattocks, ploughshares, spades, and sickles, eschewing martial labour. Bees bring honey rather than harm, in Flight's moral image. The devil's visit and the shoeing that follows explain the charm. The tale mixes saint's legend with folk custom. It charms readers of folklore and Cruikshank illustration.
14568-sir-gawayne-and-the-green-knight-a:
Richard Morris re-edited Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight, an alliterative romance poem of about 1360, from Cotton manuscript Nero A.x. in the British Museum, in a second edition revised in 1869. Morris had edited Early English Alliterative Poems.

The poem tells how a green knight challenges Arthur's court, Gawayne takes up the axe, and a year later seeks the adventure he promised, feasting and arming along the way. Morris checked his text against Sir Frederic Madden's edition and the manuscript. The volume is a foundational scholarly edition of a masterpiece of Middle English verse.
14892-daniel-defoe:
William Minto's life of Daniel Defoe sits in the English Men of Letters series, edited by John Morley. It places Defoe among Johnson, Gibbon, Scott, Shelley, Hume, Goldsmith and Burns, each treated by a leading critic. Minto follows Defoe from trade and business through politics, journalism and fiction.

Chapters trace what businesses, what trade and what part of the world shaped a writer who turned pamphlets, projects and novels into a career. Defoe emerges as a practical man of letters, always writing for a market and a cause. Minto's short life remains a clear introduction to an author whose most famous book, Robinson Crusoe, was only one product of a restless working life.
1919-grand-ther-baldwin-s-thanksgiving-w:
Horatio Alger Jr. 's Ballads, published in 1875, gathers his poems around the title piece, Grand'ther Baldwin's Thanksgiving, with St. Nicholas, Barbara's Courtship, The Confession, and John Maynard among the ballads, and miscellaneous poems including In the Church at Stratford-on-Avon.

The verses are plain, sentimental, and earnest, in Alger's usual manner, with young love burning brightest and purest in field, hamlet, or crowded mart. Readers who know Alger's novels for boys will recognize the same morals in verse: honesty, gratitude, and work rewarded. The book is a period piece, but its best ballads still carry a tune.
19957-facing-the-german-foe:
Colonel James Fiske titled his boys' war book Facing the German Foe in 1915. A young recruit marvels that his new comrades speak his language. You do say some funny things, though, old chap, he admits. Mr. Grenfel let him join the troop right away, to his surprise. The scene is a British troop welcoming an American boy. Fiske wrote the Great War for young readers while it raged.

America was neutral in 1915, but its boys read war hungrily. Fiske's series put American youths inside the Allied armies. Language jokes ease the plunge into trenches. The foe of the title is faced early and often. Such books shaped a generation's war imagination. They are period pieces of mobilized boyhood.
20744-mary-s-peake-the-colored-teacher-a:
Mary S. Peake taught freed children at Fortress Monroe during the Civil War, and this short life tells her story. Her uncle John Paine was freed by a kind man who bought slaves to set them free. Mary grew up as a pet of that household, treated almost like a daughter.

Peake's school work under Union guns made her a famed figure in Black education. The book keeps her faith, care, and early death before the reader. It is brief, but it kept her name alive when few Black teachers were honored in print. Readers meet a quiet hero of the war years.
21787-shelled-by-an-unseen-foe:
Boys at a military school feel the pull of the Great War in this 1916 novel by Colonel James Fiske. It is volume eight of the World's War Series. The tallest of three friends announces that he is going home. Ripping times are promised there. His father and brothers are already in the field, and one brother was shot in the trenches in France.

The chapters carry the young men from school into service, through struggle, letters home, and days of waiting. A bit of romance and a girl named Helen soften the war's edge. Fiske wrote while the war still raged, for boys who expected to follow. It is a period piece of wartime youth fiction, earnest and brisk.
22347-through-canal-land-in-a-canadian-c:
Through Canal Land in a Canadian Canoe follows a pleasure trip by water. The travelers spent three weeks on their planned route. The day fixed for the start found them in high spirits.

All arrangements stood complete when that morning came. The party overflowed with cheerful hopes for the good time ahead. Health and spirits, the account says, were at their best. Canal travel by canoe mixed ease with slow adventure. Such trips let holiday makers see country from its waterways. Readers get a cheerful period travel record. It recalls a time when three free weeks and a canoe promised a complete escape.
25013-how-to-make-a-shoe:
Jno. P. Headley's 1882 manual, printed by Gibson Brothers in Washington, teaches shoemaking in verse as much as in prose. The opening rhymes run through the trade's materials: horse and cow leather cut up side, sheep for lining, goat, calf, and kid, with linen linings for those who feel refined. Feet need protection, the author insists, and buyers should select the best of shoemakers as well as shoes.

Headley, having passed through the scenes he describes, offers the book to craft and public alike as a text-book or family book. Measuring gets careful verse treatment. Length comes first, two sizes added to make the toe comfortable, the heel reached in perfect order, and the instep measured with half an inch off, no less and not much more. The manual is a craftsman's primer in doggerel.
28796-the-white-doe:
Sallie Southall Cotten wrote this 1901 verse legend about Virginia Dare, the first English child born in America, whose fate became the mystery of the Lost Colony. The poem tells how the lost girl is said to have lived among Native people and, in legend, to have been changed into a white doe. Cotten printed the book for herself in Philadelphia and dedicated it to the National Society of Colonial Dames.

A long prose introduction argues that studying the past, with its mistakes and successes, lights the way forward better than any guess about the future. The poem itself is romantic and patriotic in tone, treating a famous American mystery as folklore rather than fact. Readers get a period piece: an early twentieth-century retelling of the Roanoke story in flowing, old-fashioned verse.
561-the-further-adventures-of-robinson-c:
Daniel Defoe's castaway returns to sea in this sequel, written as Crusoe's own plain account. At sixty-one, rich and settled after thirty-five years of hardship, Crusoe feels the old rambling urge stir again. He revisits his island, sails on, and meets new perils, proving that what is bred in the bone will not leave the flesh.

Defoe writes in steady, practical prose, full of trade, ships, and moral reckoning. The sequel lacks the first book's tight island focus, yet it grips as a wanderer's confession. Readers will find an older Crusoe, still restless, still learning that home is hard to keep.
7799-an-american-robinson-crusoe:
Samuel B Allison's An American Robinson Crusoe retells Defoe's castaway tale for American boys and girls, with added incidents and a plain, practical bent. Contents run from Robinson with his parents and as an apprentice through shipwreck, first night on land, shelter, and a calendar kept alone.

Later chapters show him making a hat, hunting bag, shoes, and parasol. He gets fire, builds furniture, keeps goats, farms, pots, bakes, and fishes, before he builds a boat and meets savages on the shore. It is a teaching story of self-reliance, step by careful step.
8893-selections-from-poe:
J. Montgomery Gambrill, head of history and civics at Baltimore Polytechnic Institute, edits these selections from Edgar Allan Poe. A biographical and critical introduction and notes, inscribed to the school's Poe and Lowell literary societies. A portrait after Cole's engraving fronts the book, and a bibliography opens the contents. Poems follow in order: Song, Spirits of the Dead, Romance, To the River, To Science, To Helen, Israfel, The City in the Sea, The Sleeper, and Lenore.

The Valley of Unrest, The Coliseum, Hymn, To One in Paradise, Silence, The Conqueror Worm, Dream-Land, The Raven, Eulalie. Ulalume continue the poetic selection, with tales and essays beyond. Gambrill's school edition frames Poe for students, with notes that explain without dulling the mystery. Readers new to Poe get a well-chosen doorway, and teachers a classroom text that has served generations.
9179-the-bride-of-the-mistletoe:
James Lane Allen wrote this Kentucky novel of a man, a secret, and a tree at sunset. The contents list Earth Shield and Earth Festival, with chapters on the man and the secret, the lighting of candles, and a wandering tale. A room of silences and a white dawn close the pattern. Maupassant's counsel on seeing truly fronts the book.

Allen sets his tale on a mighty table-land in the south, where folk custom and nature mix. The mistletoe bride of the title hovers as symbol and fate. Readers who like brooding, poetic romance will find here a strange and haunting work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antinoe:
Antinoe, or Antinopolis, titular see of the Thebaid, now Esneh, an Egyptian city built by Hadrian in 132 for Antinous. In Egypt's centre, the city drew more than ordinary attention by its splendour and originality, built on Roman and Greek plans without Egyptian architecture. Its ruins grow yearly less distinct, as a nearby European industry draws on antique materials like a deserted marble quarry. Like Greek and Asiatic cities, it had streets lined with porticoes and colonnades, several arched over.

Antinoe played but a small part in Christian history, though it became a bishopric seat. Its dead were prepared with clothes, stuffing, and a mask instead of mummification, preserving personal effects and stuffs. Gayet's excavations brought the Musée Guimet chaplets, baskets, phials, and boxes, plus papyri including Aurelius Colluthus's will. Nearby Deïr Abou-Hennys holds an underground church with Gospel and apocryphal paintings amid mostly mutilated inscriptions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arsinoe:
Arsinoe, a titular see of Egypt now called Medinet el Fayum, capital of its district, stands on the Nile's west bank between river and Lake Moeris. It now stands on the Bahr-Youssuf, some fifty-two miles southwest of Cairo. Its bishops' list from about 250 to 649 is given in Gams. Most famous of several Egyptian cities of the name, it was favoured and renamed by Ptolemy II, who ruled from 284 to 247 BC, for his sister and wife Arsinoe.

Samaritan Jews settled there, and it soon rivalled Alexandria for vineyards and gardens on Egypt's most fertile soil, trading briskly in grain and vegetables and famed for figs and roses. For piety toward the crocodile it was called Crocodilopolis, a haunt of crocodiles. It grew into a Christian centre, but in 642 Monophysite Copts betrayed it to Amru, Arab lieutenant of Mohammed, and modern Fayum is famed for finds of 1877 to 1878.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartholomew-r:
Bartholomew Roe, called Venerable Alban, was an English Benedictine martyr born in Suffolk in 1583 and executed at Tyburn in 1641. Educated in Suffolk and at Cambridge, he was converted by a visit to a Catholic prisoner at St Albans. Admitted to Douai's English College, he was professed at Dieulward in 1612 and reached the mission in 1615.

Imprisoned from 1618 to 1623, he was banished, returned within four months, and was arrested again in 1625. After St Albans, the Fleet, and Newgate, he was condemned as a priest under Elizabeth's statute and executed. With him suffered Thomas Greene, eighty, who had lived fourteen years under sentence of death. Drawn on one hurdle, they heard each other's confessions and were hanged together amid great popular sympathy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caloe:
Caloe was a titular see of Asia Minor. It is named Kaloe and Keloue in third-century inscriptions and Kalose in Hierocles. The episcopal lists give Kalloe, Kaloe, or even Kolone, and place it between the sixth and the twelfth or thirteenth centuries. It must be the modern village of Kilis, southwest of Ala-Shehir in the upper valley of the Caÿstrus.

A Lake Koloe in Lydia stands near the tombs of Lydian kings and a temple of Artemis. It gave Lequien his guess for the see's name, but that view clashes with the lists, which make Caloe a suffragan of Ephesus. The name's origin stays unsettled between the village site and the lake.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-monroe:
Soldier and convert James Monroe was born in Albemarle County, Virginia, on 10 September 1799. He died at Orange, New Jersey, on 7 September 1870. He was son of Andrew Monroe, brother of President James Monroe, and greatly resembled his famous uncle. After West Point he graduated in 1815 and became an artillery lieutenant. In war with Algerian pirates he was wounded on 17 June 1815. He was directing guns of the frigate Guerrière off Cape de Gata, Spain.

As aide to General Scott he served from 1817 to 1822. He did garrison duty as first lieutenant of the Fourth Artillery until 30 September 1832, when he resigned. Settling in New York, he entered public life. He served on the Board of Aldermen from 1833 to 1835 and in Congress from 1839 to 1841. Nominated again in 1846, he declined to run after a contested election and a new election order. The entry presents a soldier-politician of the early republic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kerry-and-agh:
Kerry and Aghadoe is an Irish diocese covering County Kerry and part of Cork, formed by joining two ancient sees, Ardfert and Aghadoe, before the Synod of Rathbrassil in 1110. This entry gives its size at 983,400 acres and its Catholic population in 1901 at 187,346.

Tradition says St. Patrick never set foot in Kerry, blessing it from a height in Limerick instead, yet Christianity reached the county very early, as old monuments attest. Its first named bishop, Erc of Slane, who died in 512, held authority there before St. Brendan's birth and stayed for years after. Rathbrassil fixed the united see at Rathass, near Tralee.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-killaloe:
Killaloe, Irish Cill-da-Lua, is a suffragan diocese of Cashel taking in most of Clare, much of Tipperary, and parts of four other counties. This entry names it for St. Lua, a sixth-century abbot whose oratory still stands on Friar's Island, while St. Flannan, its patron, was its first bishop, consecrated at Rome around 640.

The diocese took its present shape only in the twelfth century. The Synod of Rathbresail suppressed the old sees of Roscrea and Inniscathy and folded them into Killaloe, matching roughly the old Kingdom of Thomond. Roscrea had grown around St. Cronan's monastery and famous school, where the scribe Dimma copied the Four Gospels now in Trinity College, Dublin. Inniscathy grew around St. Senan's monastery, with Senan himself as its first bishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-linoe:
Linoe was a small bishop's seat in Bithynia Secunda, a late Roman province in what is now Turkey. Old lists of bishops are the only trace of it, and they place it as a lesser see under Nicaea through the twelfth and thirteenth centuries.

Emperor Justinian likely raised the place to city rank, and the entry links it with modern Biledjik, a rail stop where silk worms were raised. About ten thousand people lived there, most of them Muslims, with three thousand Armenians, six hundred of them Catholic. Four bishops are named: Anastasius at Constantinople in 692, Leo at Nicaea in 787, and Basil and Cyril at Constantinople in 879, on opposite sides of the Ignatius and Photius split.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrick-donah:
Patrick Donahoe was a Boston publisher born at Munnery in County Cavan on 17 March 1811 and dead at Boston on 18 March 1901. He reached Boston aged ten with his parents and at fourteen began a printer's apprenticeship. He worked on The Jesuit, started by Bishop Fenwick in 1832, and carried it on with Devereaux as the Literary and Catholic Sentinel after the bishop gave it up.

In 1836 he founded The Pilot, a weekly for Irish-American and Catholic interests that became New England's organ of Catholic opinion. A publishing and book house grew beside it, issuing many Catholic books, and later he organised a bank. All ventures thrived, and his wealth generously served Catholic causes. Boston's great fire of 1872 wrecked his plant, a second fire and rash loans to friends sank his bank in 1876, but by 1881 he had bought back The Pilot.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raphoe:
The Diocese of Raphoe covers the greater part of County Donegal, in the church province of Armagh. This encyclopedia entry explains the name Rathboth, fort of cottages, and notes that Raphoe was the first of Saint Columba's Irish foundations to become an episcopal see. Columba founded its monastery in the sixth century, and Adamnan renovated it about 700, succeeding Columba at Raphoe as well as at Iona.

Adamnan died at Iona in 704, after spending his last six years in Ireland, where his mother's kindred held the Raphoe district. It is suggested that he then held episcopal orders with a seat at Raphoe. Eunan, venerated as the first bishop of Raphoe, is no other than Adamnan himself. Later prelates include Donald MacCongail, present at Trent in 1563, and a bishop transferred to Kildare in 1737, after which no Catholic bishop has resided at Raphoe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-siloe:
Siloe, also called Siloah or Siloam, is a pool in the Tyropoean Valley just outside Jerusalem's south wall, where Jesus gave sight to the man born blind. Excavations by Bliss and others put its identity with the Siloe of Isaiah and John beyond doubt. Near the traditional pool Bliss found in 1896 an ancient basin, 75 feet by 78 feet and 18 feet deep, with a church and nave on its north side.

The pool joins the upper source of Gihon's waters by a subterranean conduit 600 yards long, called the king's aqueduct, whose fall is so slight that water runs very gently. Hence Isaiah compares the House of David to the waters of Siloe that go softly. In 1880 diggers found in the pool an inscription, the oldest Hebrew writing except the Mesa stone, probably from the seventh century BC. The tower in Siloe was likely part of the nearby city wall.
first-project-gutenberg-collection-of-ed:
Edgar Allan Poe's works fill this early Project Gutenberg collection file, one of the project's first experiments in cataloguing several items together. Michael Hart's header explains the indexing experiment before the texts begin. The Raven leads, its narrator pondering weak and weary over forgotten lore until the tapping comes at his chamber door.

The Masque of the Red Death follows in the file's middle, where Prince Prospero's masked ball meets a stranger of whom no jest can be made. Poems and tales are bundled without modern editing or notes. As an artifact, the file shows digital publishing in its infancy while delivering two of Poe's most famous pieces in plain text.
grand-ther-baldwin-s-thanksgiving-with-o:
Horatio Alger Jr published his Ballads in 1875, led by Grand'ther Baldwin's Thanksgiving, a New England holiday poem of an old man's table and returning children. The contents group narrative ballads first: St Nicholas, Barbara's Courtship, The Confession, Phoebe's Wooing, and John Maynard, the wheelsman who held his burning steamer to shore. Friar Anselmo closes the group.

Miscellaneous poems visit Stratford church and Mrs Browning's grave at Florence, while a war section gathers Gone to the War, Where Is My Boy To-night, and King Cotton. Harvard odes end the book, Alger's own college loyalty showing. The verses explain his novels' hold: plain meters, strong feeling, and moral endings, by a writer America knew as a boys' storyteller.
podcast-joerogan-l_Y3tUZRvOE:
Jimmy Corsetti joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1742. Corsetti's Bright Insight channel turned him into the internet's history hunter, arguing for lost chapters of the human past. His specialty is Atlantis and the sites he says the experts misread.

He walks Rogan through the evidence he rates highest, from the Sahara's Richat Structure to drowned coasts and old maps. Rogan asks how a YouTube researcher checks himself without a university behind him. The episode is a full hearing for the amateur's case, in a studio that has done more than any other to amplify it.
selections-from-poe:
J. Montgomery Gambrill, a Baltimore school head, edited this choice of Edgar Allan Poe's work with a life sketch, critical notes, and a book list. Gambrill dedicated the volume to two literary societies of the Baltimore Polytechnic Institute. A portrait of Poe, after an engraving by Cole, fronts the book.

The poem list runs from Song and Spirits of the Dead through The Raven, Lenore, and Ulalume. Tales and essays follow the verse in the full contents. Students meet Poe's dark music and strange fancy in a school-ready set, guided by notes that explain his life and the pull of his art.
sir-gawayne-and-the-green-knight-an-alli:
Richard Morris re-edited this alliterative romance poem, dated about 1360, from the Cotton manuscript Nero A.x in the British Museum. Morris had edited Hampole's Pricke of Conscience and other early English poems. His preface thanks Sir F. Madden's Syr Gawayne for a text so accurate that copying labor was spared.

Morris read Madden's copy against the manuscript and checked proof sheets as they came. This revised second edition expands the manuscript's short forms and adds side notes so readers can follow the tale. A glossary from Madden, enlarged by Morris, helps with the hard northern tongue of Gawayne's adventures.
the-bride-of-the-mistletoe:
James Lane Allen wrote The Bride of the Mistletoe. Allen had also written Flute and Violin, A Kentucky Cardinal, and Aftermath. Its chapters are The Man and the Secret, The Tree and the Sunset, and The Lighting of the Candles. The Wandering Tale, The Room of the Silences, and The White Dawn follow.

The prose opens with a mighty table-land that lies southward in a hardy region of the country. It has the form of a vast shield, broken in some outlines and rude of make. Nature forged it for some crisis in her long war of time and change, used it, and left it as an old war piece. That shield is Kentucky.
the-further-adventures-of-robinson-cruso:
Daniel Defoe's hero tells The Further Adventures of Robinson Crusoe in his own voice, picking up his tale at the age of sixty-one. Age and wealth, he owns, could not cure his urge to roam.

Crusoe grants he had money enough and no need to seek more. Yet the wish to see his island and the colony he left there ran in his head day and night. He talked of it in his sleep and bored all company with it. Defoe sends his old sailor back to sea, to the island, and on to fresh trades and perils in far lands, still ruled by the rambling bent of his youth.
the-horse-shoe:
Edward G. Flight wrote The True Legend of St. Dunstan and the Devil, showing how the horse-shoe came to be a charm against witchcraft, catalogued here under the short title The Horse Shoe. The third edition is dated 1871, with illustrations by George Cruikshank engraved by John Thompson. A preface to the second edition opens the book.

Flight credits the success of the first edition in great part to the eminent artists who drew and engraved the pictures. To have given innocent amusement without pain, he says, is enjoyment well worth writing for, and fresh friendships around so small a trifle make the reward larger still.
the-solitary-of-juan-fernandez-or-the-re: The Solitary of Juan Fernandez, or The Real Robinson Crusoe, is credited only to the author of Picciola. Anne T. Wilbur translated it from the French. The date printed is 1851. The pages shown give a detailed contents list and no narrative text. Chapter one names Captain Stradling, William Dampier, and Miss Catherine's reveries. The tour of the world and Selkirk's revolt follow. Later chapters treat the colonist's labors, his hammock, and an invasion of the island.
